summary: The data used to study fires over the last 25 years were collected by older satellite sensors, MODIS, and they cannot simply be combined with data from the newer VIIRS sensors, because the two differ in their characteristics and in their observation schedules. We brought the data from all the satellites to one common form, made sure no detection is counted twice where the satellites overlap, and built a map where anyone can look at any area for any period, based on all the data we could find. It is made for emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and scientists, so they can get the most accurate data for their work.

Live site: https://nasa.pin-planet.org

Code: https://github.com/Left2Bad/NASA-Hackaton-Catharsis-team

Video (30 s): https://youtu.be/tdj4Dv01Lrs

Slides (PDF): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ddteLKIbTuUwZlcC62qwqidlGcDI4hgb/view?usp=sharing

Data. We started by collecting all the data available: 48 yearly FIRMS archives, about 10 GB, plus the fresh, still incomplete data for 2026 from the FIRMS Area API (we had to split the requests into many small pieces to download everything). All detections go onto one grid of 0.1° cells, day by day.

Harmonization. Each 1° cell gets its own coefficient that converts MODIS to the VIIRS scale; where a cell has little data, the coefficient is pulled toward its 5° block and toward the world value. Volcanoes, gas flares and industrial heat sources are masked out. On days when the lead satellite sent no data, another satellite fills in.

Check. The coefficients are fitted on 2012–2020 and tested on 2021–2025, years the method never saw: VIIRS is predicted from MODIS alone and compared with what VIIRS really recorded.

Northern Kazakhstan: bias −8.8 %, median monthly error 19.9 %.

Southern Amazon: bias −0.3 %, median monthly error 16.3 %.

Northern California: bias +4.2 %, median monthly error 21.4 %.

Joined as they are, the records jump ×3.80 at 2012 worldwide; in the harmonized record the ratio is 0.97.

The web application. Pick an example, draw a rectangle or polygon, or type coordinates, and choose the years. You get a calendar of every month since November 2000 (detections, anomalies against the median, or the sensors as they recorded), the current month against the median of the same days in 25 years, the season profile, yearly totals with the trend, a daily calendar, hot spots on the map colored by fire power, and downloads: CSV of the hot spots and of the monthly table, PNG charts. The color scales are checked for three kinds of color blindness.

Built with: NASA FIRMS data (MODIS and VIIRS 375 m), a Python pipeline, FastAPI + DuckDB, React + MapLibre. Open source, Apache 2.0.
